title: Keeping many values
objectives: Track a running maximum in a loop, stop early with `break`, and handle an empty list.

screens.title: Picking one value out
screens.prose:
A list keeps five closing prices in order. Square brackets after its name pick one value out.

```python
prices = [101.20, 99.80, 103.50, 102.10, 104.75]
print(prices[2])
```
screens.question: Tap the value `prices[2]` refers to.

hints.text: Does Python count positions from 0 or from 1?
`prices[0]` is the first value, 101.20.
Count 0, 1, 2 from the left: `prices[2]` is the third value, 103.50.

feedback.correct: Counting from 0, position 2 is the third price, 103.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Number the positions from 0, starting at the left.

byKey.c1: You counted from 1. Python numbers positions from 0, so `prices[2]` is the third value.
byKey.c3: You counted one too far. Positions run 0, 1, 2 from the left.

explain.text: The number in square brackets is the **index**: the position, counted from 0. `prices[0]` is 101.20, the first price, so `prices[2]` is 103.50, the third.

screens.title: From the end, and how many
screens.prose:
Two more ways to look at a list: a negative index counts from the end, and `len` counts the values.

```python
prices = [101.20, 99.80, 103.50, 102.10, 104.75]
print(prices[-1], len(prices))
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You gave the last index, 4. `len` counts the values, and there are 5.
You read `-1` as the first value. A negative index counts from the end, so `-1` is the last.

options.text: An error: there is no index −1
options.why: Negative indexes are allowed. `-1` is the last value, `-2` the one before.

hints.text: Which value is one step back from the start, wrapping round to the end?
`prices[-1]` is the last value. `len(prices)` counts all of them.
The last price is 104.75, and there are 5 prices.

feedback.correct: The last value, and a count of 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `-1` counts from the end; `len` counts every value.

explain.text: `prices[-1]` is the last value, 104.75, and `len(prices)` is 5. The indexes run 0 to 4, so the last index is always one less than the length.

screens.title: Building and changing a list
screens.prose:
Lists can grow and change. `append` adds a value at the end; assigning to an index replaces that value.

```python
closes = []
closes.append(99.80)
closes.append(101.25)
closes[0] = 100.00
print(closes)
```
screens.question: What does the last line print?

options.why: You treated `closes[0] = ...` as adding. Assigning to an index replaces the value already there.
You inserted at the front. `closes[0] = 100.00` overwrites position 0; nothing moves.
You replaced the second value. Index 0 is the first.

hints.text: After the two appends, what is at index 0?
Assigning to `closes[0]` overwrites the first value.
The list is [99.8, 101.25], then index 0 becomes 100.0: [100.0, 101.25].

feedback.correct: The first value is replaced; the length stays 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `append` adds at the end; `closes[0] = ...` replaces the first value.

explain.text: The appends build `[99.8, 101.25]`. Then `closes[0] = 100.00` replaces the first value, so the list stays two long. Python prints floats without trailing zeros, as `100.0`.

screens.title: The highest price so far
screens.prose:
To find the highest price, keep the best one seen so far and replace it whenever a higher price comes along. Step through.

```python
prices = [100.00, 104.00, 101.50, 106.20, 103.00]
peak = prices[0]
for p in prices:
    if p > peak:
        peak = p
print(peak)
```

steps.caption: Before the loop: `peak = prices[0]`, 100.00. Pass 1 compares 100.00 with itself, so nothing changes.
Pass 2: 104.00 is above the peak, so `peak` becomes 104.00.
Pass 3: 101.50 is not above 104.00, so `peak` stays.
Pass 4: 106.20 is above the peak, so `peak` becomes 106.20.
Pass 5: 103.00 is not above 106.20, so `peak` stays. The loop ends and `print(peak)` shows 106.2.

screens.title: When does the peak move?
screens.prose:
The same loop on a new price list.

```python
prices = [50.00, 48.00, 52.00, 52.00, 55.00, 51.00]
peak = prices[0]
for p in prices:
    if p > peak:
        peak = p
```
screens.question: Tap every price at which `peak` changes.

hints.text: `peak` starts at 50.00. Walk right and ask: is this price strictly above the peak?
Look at the second 52.00. Is it above a peak of 52.00?
52.00 beats 50.00, and 55.00 beats 52.00. The first price, the 48.00, the repeat 52.00 and the 51.00 change nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap a price only when it is strictly above the peak so far.

byKey.ties: The second 52.00 equals the peak. `52.0 > 52.0` is `False`, so nothing changes.
byKey.first: `peak` already starts at the first price, so pass 1 changes nothing.
byKey.c3: The second 52.00 equals the peak. `52.0 > 52.0` is `False`, so nothing changes.

explain.text: The peak moves at 52.00 and again at 55.00. A price equal to the peak fails `p > peak`, so ties change nothing. The peak ends at 55.00, the list's highest price.

screens.title: A best day that never happened
screens.prose:
Every day this week lost money. A colleague looks for the best day, but starts `best` at 0.

```python
pnls = [-120.00, -45.50, -80.00]
best = 0
for p in pnls:
    if p > best:
        best = p
print(best)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: That is the best day, but `best` starts at 0 and no loss is above 0. The loop never changes it.
You started from the first P&L. This code starts `best` at 0 instead.
You added the days up. The loop keeps the largest, not the total.

hints.text: Is any of these P&Ls above 0?
`best` only changes when `p > best`. It starts at 0.
Every P&L is negative, so `p > 0` is False each time. `best` stays 0.

feedback.correct: No loss beats 0, so `best` never moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether `p > best` is ever True when `best` starts at 0.

byKey.largest: You found the right best day by eye. The code starts at 0, which beats every loss, so it prints 0.

explain.text:
Starting at 0 invents a P&L of £0 that was never in the list, and it beats every loss. Start from a real value, `best = pnls[0]`, so the answer is always one of the days. Here that gives −45.5.

```python
best = pnls[0]     # a real value, not 0
for p in pnls:
    if p > best:
        best = p
```

canvas.caption: Best day: −45.50, found only when best starts at pnls[0]

screens.title: The largest value, safely
screens.prose: Write the running-maximum loop yourself. An empty list has no largest value, and `values[0]` would stop with an `IndexError`. So check the length first, and return `None` for an empty list.
screens.question: Complete `largest`.

widget.starter:
def largest(values):
    best = None
    # if values is not empty, set best to the
    # largest value; otherwise leave it None
    
    return best
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. An empty list must return `None`, Python's value for 'nothing'.

hints.text: Guard everything with one `if` that checks the list is not empty.
Inside that `if`: start `best` at `values[0]`, then loop with an `if v > best:` inside.
Write `if len(values) > 0:`, then `best = values[0]`, then `for v in values:` with `if v > best:` and `best = v` nested inside.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed, the empty list and the all-negative list included.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Try `largest([])` by hand: it must not touch `values[0]`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. If it is an `IndexError`, `values[0]` ran on the empty list: put it inside the length check.

screens.title: Stopping early
screens.prose:
A risk check walks through daily returns, in %, and stops at the first day below −2.0. `break` ends a loop at once.

```python
returns = [0.4, -0.8, 1.1, -2.6, 0.9, -3.1]
for r in returns:
    if r < -2.0:
        print("limit hit", r)
        break
    print("ok", r)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You carried on after `break`. It ends the whole loop, so the last two days are never looked at.
You finished the pass after `break`. It leaves at once, so `ok -2.6` never prints.
You stopped at the first loss. −0.8 is not below −2.0, so it passes.

hints.text: Which is the first return below −2.0?
Every pass before that one prints `ok`.
0.4, −0.8 and 1.1 print `ok`. −2.6 is below −2.0, so it prints `limit hit -2.6` and `break` ends the loop.

feedback.correct: Three `ok` lines, then the limit, then nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the list and stop for good at the first return below −2.0.

byKey.carry-on: You carried on after `break`. It ends the whole loop, not just that pass.

explain.text: The `if` sits inside the loop, and `break` sits inside the `if`. At −2.6 the test is `True`, so the limit line prints and `break` leaves the loop. The days after it, 0.9 and −3.1, are never checked.

screens.title: Lists in one place
screens.prose:
A list of length $n$ has indexes $0$ to $n - 1$, and `-1` is the last. A running peak follows $\text{peak}_t = \max(\text{peak}_{t-1},\ p_t)$, starting from $\text{peak}_0 = p_0$.

```python
x = prices[0]          # first value
y = prices[-1]         # last value
n = len(prices)        # how many
prices.append(99.50)   # add at the end
prices[0] = 100.00     # replace the first
```
screens.question: A list has 8 values. What is the index of its last value?

options.why: That is the length. Indexes start at 0, so the last is one less.
That counts from the end with a positive number. The last value is at index 7, or −1.
`prices[-8]` is the first value of an 8-long list, not the last.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Indexes start at 0, so subtract one from the length.

explain.text: With 8 values the indexes run 0 to 7. `prices[7]` and `prices[-1]` are the same value. `prices[8]` stops with an `IndexError`.

screens.prose: Risk teams track how far a price sits below its highest point so far. The first ingredient is the running peak: one value per day, the highest close up to and including that day.
screens.question: Complete `running_peak` so it returns the list of peaks.

widget.starter:

    peaks = []
    # for each price, append the highest
    # price seen so far to peaks
    
    return peaks
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. The result has one value per price, in order; an empty list gives `[]`.

hints.text: This is the running maximum, plus one `append` per day.
The `append` belongs inside the `for` block but outside the `if`: every day adds a peak, changed or not.
Inside `if len(prices) > 0:` start `peak = prices[0]`. Loop `for p in prices:`, update `peak` when `p > peak`, then `peaks.append(peak)` at the loop's indent.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed: one peak per day, never falling.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the length: the result needs one value for every price.

byKey.test-1: Check that you append on every day, not only when the peak changes.

ideas: Indexes count from 0: `x[0]` is the first value, `x[-1]` the last, and `len(x)` the count.
A running maximum starts at a real value, `x[0]`, and replaces it whenever a value is strictly larger.
`break` ends a loop at once; check `len(x) > 0` before touching `x[0]`, because an empty list has no first value.

formula.name: Running peak
formula.note: The gap $\text{peak}_t - p_t$ is the drawdown on day $t$.

summary.trap: Starting a maximum at 0 invents a value: for a list of losses it returns 0, not the best loss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Index 1 is the second value; index −1 is the last.

byKey.from-one: You took `x[1]` as the first value, 4. Index 1 is the second value, 8.
byKey.neg-second-last: You took `x[-1]` as 15. Index −1 is the last value, 16.

explain.text: Indexes count from 0, so `x[1]` is 8. `x[-1]` is the last value, 16. Their sum is 24.

options.text: It prints `0`, then stops with an `IndexError`.

options.why: An empty list has no value at index 0, so Python cannot print one.
Python does not fill in missing values. Asking for one is an error.

options.text: It stops with an error before printing anything.
options.why: `len([])` is fine: it is 0. Only the second line fails.

feedback.correct: `len` of an empty list is 0; index 0 does not exist.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the two lines one at a time.

explain.text: `len(prices)` is 0, so the first line prints `0`. `prices[0]` asks for a first value that is not there, so Python stops with `IndexError: list index out of range`. Check the length before indexing.

quiz.prose:
```python
count = 0
for p in [3, -1, 4, -5, 9]:
    if p < -2:
        break
    count = count + 1
print(count)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

widget.label: Value printed
widget.accept: 3: the passes for 3, −1 and 4 count; −5 breaks.

feedback.correct: 3, −1 and 4 are counted; −5 ends the loop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop for good at the first value below −2.

byKey.counted-break: You counted −5. `break` comes before `count = count + 1`, so that pass adds nothing.
byKey.no-break: You counted every value. `break` ends the loop at −5.
byKey.skipped-neg: −1 is not below −2, so it is counted.

explain.text: 3, −1 and 4 all pass, so `count` reaches 3. At −5 the test is `True` and `break` leaves before the count line. 9 is never seen.

quiz.prose: You want the lowest price in a list of share prices, all above £0, with a loop that keeps `low` and replaces it with any smaller price.
quiz.question: What should `low` start as?

options.why: No price is below 0, so `low` would stay 0, a price that never happened.
That only works while every price is below a million. Start from a real value and the loop works for any prices.
That is a count, not a price. It could be below every price and never be replaced.

feedback.correct: Start from a real value in the list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick a start that is one of the prices.

explain.text: Starting from a value in the list means the answer is always a real price. Starting at 0 is the mirror of the lesson's trap: nothing is below it, so it never moves.
